prize_parts.citation: for showing how collateral constraints and asset prices amplify and propagate shocks, and so generate credit cycles

statement.case_for: Kiyotaki and Moore (1997) give a tractable dynamic general-equilibrium mechanism: borrowing limits tied to collateral values and asset prices turn small, temporary shocks into large and persistent fluctuations. The idea is general and clean. It became the base layer of financial-friction macro models, and the post-2008 policy literature built on it. Nearly three decades of extension and use settle the maturity question. Attribution is also unusually clean, because the 1997 paper is the singular origin of the mechanism and the two-person credit follows directly from it. This candidate stayed at the top of my opening ranking after I read the colleagues' openings. Six of ten members who ranked it put it first, and independent assessments of attribution and maturity converged. I treat that as a check on my own reading, not as evidence of merit.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is overlap with the 2022 prize to Bernanke, Diamond and Dybvig for work on banks and financial crises. A committee could reasonably judge that financial frictions in macro have been honoured and that the marginal contribution is smaller. The direct empirical identification of the collateral channel is also harder than the theory suggests, and the strongest evidence is indirect, from crisis episodes and calibrated models. If the committee wants a broader foundation, B005 is a stronger case on breadth of confirmation.

responses.point: Hjalmarsson ranks B011 first but proposes Kiyotaki, Moore and Gertler. She argues that Gertler's financial-accelerator and monetary-policy work has independent standing, even though Bernanke's share of the accelerator was recognised in 2022.
responses.response: I take the point that Gertler's contributions are real and independent of Bernanke's. But the discovery we would be citing is the collateral-price feedback mechanism, and that is Kiyotaki and Moore's. The accelerator works through borrower net worth and external finance premia. It is a related mechanism with different microfoundations, not a component of this one. Adding Gertler stretches the citation across two mechanisms and invites exactly the 2022 overlap objection. Gertler also appears under B019, so crediting him here muddies attribution across both entries. I would keep the two-person award unless the committee deliberately wants a broader financial-frictions citation.

responses.point: Fredriksson ranks B019, the New Keynesian framework, first, because it is the dominant working framework in academic and central-bank macro and has been tested through several policy regimes.
responses.response: The practical reach of B019 is hard to overstate, and I ranked it third myself. My reservation is attribution. Eight credited names, a three-person cap and a split between pricing, rules, synthesis and estimation mean any trio omits decisive contributors. His own opening acknowledges this. The post-2021 inflation episode and the heterogeneous-agent critiques also leave the verdict on the representative-agent version less settled. B011 loses less to the cap. I would not discount B019 on influence, but I think the attribution problem makes it a weaker prize configuration this year.

responses.point: Boppart ranks B001, Mian and Sufi on household debt, first and B011 only seventh. He cites overlap with the 2022 prize and with B001, and values the credible granular evidence on household leverage.
responses.response: I agree that Mian and Sufi's empirical identification is strong and that the policy relevance is clear. But the household-debt programme sits partly downstream of the collateral and balance-sheet mechanism. Kiyotaki-Moore is the general principle, and Mian-Sufi is a well-identified empirical application to household credit in one episode. On the overlap point, the 2022 prize concerned bank runs and the role of banks in crises, not collateral-driven amplification in the real economy. B001 is also more recent, and the disputed weight of credit supply versus other housing-boom explanations is still open. I would keep B001 as a later candidate, not as a reason to demote B011.

responses.point: Friberg ranks B005, heterogeneous-firm trade, first. He argues it is foundational and general, with two decades of confirmation, and that it underpins a large empirical and policy literature.
responses.response: B005 has the broadest top-three support, and I rank it second. I do not dismiss it. Melitz (2003) is a strong central contribution, and Helpman's role is well supported. My difference is on two points. First, Krugman's 2008 prize covered the monopolistic-competition framework this builds on, and Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum are not credited, so priority is contestable. Second, B011 has a cleaner attribution story. I see the two as close and I name B005 as my first alternative. If colleagues find the 2022 overlap decisive against B011, B005 is where I would go.

uncertainties: How heavily the committee should weigh the 2022 financial-crisis prize against the distinct collateral-amplification mechanism.
Whether adding Gertler (and possibly Gilchrist) would improve or blur the citation, given Gertler's presence in B019.
How much indirect empirical identification of the collateral channel should count against a foundational theory contribution.
Whether the 'about 15 possible prizes' tournament logic favours B005's breadth of support over B011's concentrated first-place support.
statement.conflict_note: No connection to the credited names (Kiyotaki, Moore, Gertler, Gilchrist) is apparent from the supplied profile. My own research is in macroeconomic theory (heterogeneous-agent macro, growth, climate-economy modelling), so B011 is in an adjacent field. I also have long-standing co-authorship with committee colleagues John Hassler and Timo Boppart, but neither is a credited candidate here. I disclose this for completeness and have applied the common criteria.
